segments.text: Good afternoon. The note on the booking says nose problems and a nasal spray you can't seem to put down. Is that about right?
That's right, and I'd like to be quick about it, I've got my bridge group at three and I'm already running behind.
I'm Rosa, I help Mrs. Delgado at home four days a week. I drove her, so we can only blame me if we're late.
Nice to meet you, Rosa. So, Mrs. Delgado, tell me what the nose is doing.
It's blocked. Always blocked. I can't breathe through it unless I use the spray, and then it's fine for an hour, maybe two, and then it's blocked again.
How often are you reaching for that spray?
Three or four times a day. Sometimes in the night too, I keep it right by the lamp.
And how long has the nose been stuffed up like this?
Oh, goodness. I don't know. A long time. Rosa, when did it start?
I honestly couldn't say. It was already bad when I started with you, but you'd told me it was bothering you before that, so I don't know where it began.
Could have been last winter. Could have been the winter before. I really can't pin it down, doctor.
That's fine, we'll work with that. Anything else going on, like mucus down the back of the throat?
Yes, there's a drip down the back of my throat at night, and I wake up coughing and clearing it. That's new, that's more recent.
Any fever lately? Or nosebleeds?
No fever. No nosebleeds either, thank goodness, I've got good linens and I'd like to keep them that way.
Okay. Let me make sure I have your medicines right. What are you using?
The nasal spray, the oxymetazoline one. Then amlodipine, 5 mg, one a day. And metformin, 500 mg, twice a day with food.
I put the pills in the box on Sundays, so I know she takes those. The spray is the one I can't keep track of.

Think of that spray like a rubber band. Every time you use it, the blood vessels in your nose clamp down, and when it wears off they spring back wider than before. After a while they stay stretched and swollen.
So the thing that helps is the thing that's making it worse?
Pretty much. We call it rebound. Now, what are the amlodipine and metformin for?
The amlodipine is for my high blood pressure, and the metformin is for type 2 diabetes. And the stomach acid, I get that too, I've had acid reflux for years.
Good to know. Any allergies I should be aware of? To medicines, or anything else?
I don't think so.

Well, wait. At the dentist two years ago she came out in something, a rash, maybe, after the numbing stuff. They weren't sure if it was the numbing stuff or her nerves. So possibly allergic, but we never found out.
Oh, that. I'd forgotten that. I was so cross that day.
Okay, I'll note that as a possible reaction we haven't pinned down. We can sort that out properly. Let me take a look inside your nose. Tip your head back for me.
The lining inside is red and swollen, and there's no sign of bleeding.
Is that from the spray?
Most likely it's rebound congestion from the spray, yes. Let me check your numbers quickly. Blood pressure is 138 over 82, and oxygen saturation is 97 percent.
Is the blood pressure all right? Sometimes it goes up when I'm hurried.
It's a little up, nothing to worry about today. Here's my plan. I'd like to order an HbA1c blood test, because I don't have a recent sugar reading for you.
I can bring her fasting on Thursday if that helps.
It doesn't need fasting, any morning is fine. I also want to book allergy skin testing, so we can settle that dentist question once and for all.
A needle? I don't like needles.
Just tiny pricks on the forearm. Nothing like a blood draw. And if the nose isn't better after we get you off the spray, I'd consider a CT scan of the sinuses, but I'm not doing that now.
Fine. So what do I do about the spray itself? I can't just stop.
Cut it down slowly. Use it in one nostril only for a week, leave the other one alone, and rinse both with warm salt water a couple of times a day.
I'll set a timer on my phone for the rinses.
Good Lord, the things you do at my age. Will I see you again?
Yes, I'd like to see you in three weeks, and we'll see how the nose has settled. Rosa, you're welcome to come along.
All right. Now I really must run, doctor, the cards won't deal themselves.
